architects: KTS Nguyen Van A, KTS Tran Thi B
lead: A 45-storey landmark tower rising above the Saigon River, redefining the Ho Chi Minh City skyline with a sculptural faceted facade and integrated passive-cooling systems.
photo1_cap: Triple-height atrium — natural light penetrates deep into the floor plate
photo2_cap: The faceted glass skin responds to solar angles and river views
photo3_cap: Fritted glass panels reduce solar heat gain by 40%
narrative1: The design brief called for a gateway building to the new financial district — one that acknowledged the scale of the surrounding neighbourhood while asserting a civic presence on the river.||Passive strategies including cross-ventilation shafts, external shading fins, and a planted roof reduce mechanical load by 35%, earning LEED Gold certification.
narrative2: The tower's form emerged from a solar study: each facade panel is angled to maximise panoramic views northward while deflecting direct afternoon sun. A continuous public colonnade at ground level extends the riverside promenade through the site.||Upper floors house serviced apartments with river-facing terraces; the podium contains co-working, retail, and a rooftop garden accessible to the public on weekends.

architects: KTS Le Thi D, KTS Pham Van E
lead: A 12-hectare riverside masterplan that transforms a former industrial waterfront into a continuous ecological and recreational corridor for West Hanoi.
photo1_cap: Bird's-eye view — 12 ha of open green space stitched into the urban fabric
photo2_cap: Restored wetland edges — habitat for migratory waterbirds
photo3_cap: Inclusive play zone — natural timber and sensory planting for all ages
narrative1: The site retained a latent network of drainage channels beneath decades of industrial fill. Working with local ecologists, the team chose to reveal and amplify this hidden hydrology as the armature for the entire masterplan.||Phase one prioritises habitat restoration and pedestrian connectivity. Phases two and three layer in cultural programming, a riverside amphitheatre, and a community market hall.
narrative2: Movement through the park is organised around a central spine linking the metro entrance to the river, with branching paths leading to quieter garden rooms. Cyclists share dedicated lanes separated from pedestrians by low native-grass strips.||A restrained lighting strategy illuminates wetland edges and key pavilion structures, extending the park's usable life into the evening without disturbing nesting birds.
highlights: Restores 3.2 ha of degraded wetland habitat|12 km of new pedestrian and cycling paths|Four all-season community pavilions|Phased: ecology first — culture and recreation to follow

lead: A 2 400 m² research library and digital fabrication lab designed to support the next generation of architects and engineers working at the intersection of BIM and physical making.
photo1_cap: Double-height reading room — exposed CLT structure and full-height glazing
photo3_cap: and 3D printers arranged around a central review table
narrative2: Materials archive — 1 200 samples organised by material family and thermal performance
highlights: The brief asked for a space that would blur the boundary between digital design and physical fabrication — a place where a model built in Revit could be held in the hand within the same afternoon.||Exposed cross-laminated timber structure keeps the interior warm while expressing the material honesty central to the library's pedagogical mission. All structural members are sized to be fabricated on the CNC routers housed within the building itself.
specs: Narrow floor plates maximise daylight penetration to every workspace. A roof lantern over the double-height reading room introduces controlled northern light, while deep timber fins on the east and west facades prevent direct glare during working hours.||The materials archive — open to the public three days a week — has become an unexpected civic resource, attracting product designers and builders from across the city.

architects: KTS Nguyen Thi G, KTS Bui Van H
lead: Sixty villas scattered across a forested headland on Phu Quoc's northern coast — each oriented to frame a private sea view while minimising clearance of the existing tree canopy.
photo1_cap: Infinity pool and terrace — each villa positioned to capture an unobstructed sea view
photo2_cap: Rooftops blend into the forest canopy — only 8% of existing trees removed
photo3_cap: Central restaurant pavilion — open on three sides to capture prevailing sea breezes
narrative1: The site's topography — a series of ridges descending steeply to a private beach — shaped the entire planning strategy. Rather than terracing the land, the design threads narrow access paths between existing trees, placing each villa on a minimal concrete platform that touches the ground as lightly as possible.||Locally sourced materials — basalt stone from Phu Quoc's central quarry and reclaimed timber from a demolished warehouse in Rach Gia — anchor the resort to its setting and reduced embodied carbon by an estimated 28% compared with imported alternatives.
narrative2: Water is managed in a closed loop: grey water from each villa is treated in a constructed wetland behind the restaurant pavilion and reused for landscape irrigation. Rainwater harvested from villa roofs supplies toilet flushing throughout the dry season.||The resort operates on 100% renewable electricity, supplied by a 480 kWp rooftop solar array and a battery storage system sized to cover three days of base load without grid draw.
highlights: 60 villas — each with private pool and unobstructed sea view|Only 8% of existing tree canopy removed|100% renewable electricity — 480 kWp solar + 3-day battery storage|Closed-loop water cycle: constructed wetland + rainwater harvesting

architects: KTS Tran Van I, KTS Do Thi K
lead: A 220-hectare mixed-use masterplan for Binh Duong's new administrative centre — a walkable, transit-oriented district planned around a network of canals, parks, and civic buildings.
photo1_cap: 220 ha centred on the new civic canal — rendered from the northeast
photo2_cap: The civic axis terminates at the new provincial assembly building
photo3_cap: Canal-side promenade — active ground-floor uses line both banks
narrative1: Binh Duong's rapid industrial growth had outpaced its civic infrastructure. The provincial government sought a new administrative centre that would also function as a genuine public destination — a place residents would choose to visit on weekends, not just on official business.||The masterplan organises 220 hectares around a central canal corridor, with a civic axis of government buildings, a cultural museum, and a public library terminating at a large central park. Medium-density residential and mixed-use blocks step down in height toward the canal edges.
narrative2: Transit is prioritised throughout: a dedicated BRT spine connects the district to existing Binh Duong bus routes, and all residential plots are within 500 m of a BRT stop. Ground-floor retail is mandated on all streets facing the canal and civic axis, ensuring active frontages at all hours.||Flood resilience is embedded in the canal network itself: the waterways are sized to handle a 1-in-100-year storm event, with upstream retention basins in the northern park preventing overland flow from reaching the civic core.
highlights: 220 ha mixed-use district designed around a central canal network|All residential plots within 500 m of a BRT stop|Canal network sized for 1-in-100-year storm resilience|Active ground-floor retail mandated on all canal-facing streets
